analysis.one_liner: Bans unregulated soft money for national parties and tightens campaign disclosure, penalties, and officeholder fundraising rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 23, 1998 by Representative Charles Bass with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten campaign finance rules. It would have stopped national party committees from raising or spending unregulated "soft money" — the large, unlimited contributions that sat outside federal limits and disclosure — and required state and local parties to pay for federal election work only with regulated, reported money. It would have required the FEC to post campaign reports on the internet within 24 hours, cut the threshold for naming donors in reports from $200 to $50, tightened the rules for so-called issue ads run in coordination with candidates, doubled penalties for violations, banned fundraising on federal property by the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress, stopped Members from converting campaign money to personal use, restricted taxpayer-funded election-year mailings, and strengthened the ban on foreign money. It was introduced in April 1998, shortly after the 1996 election's campaign finance controversies, and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and small donors would gain the most: campaign reports posted online within 24 hours, donors named in public filings starting at $50, an end to party soft money, faster disclosure of independent spending near elections, doubled penalties for violations, and a ban on fundraising by federal officials on government property. Shareholders and union members would gain the right to a separate, revocable written consent and annual objection before their money funds political activity. Candidates who cap their own spending at $50,000 would get certification as eligible candidates, and law-abiding campaigns would benefit from clearer, mandatory late-filing penalties applying evenly to everyone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, shareholders, and union members

how_it_helps.text: It bans national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or directing unregulated soft money, and requires state and local party committees to fund all federal election activity out of regulated, reported hard money.

It requires the FEC to post every electronically filed campaign report on the internet within 24 hours, and lowers the contributor-identification threshold from $200 to $50 so more small donors and their addresses appear in public filings.

It defines 'express advocacy' and 'coordination with a candidate' in statute, closing part of the issue-advertising loophole by treating coordinated payments as regulated contributions and requiring 24- to 48-hour reports of independent spending near elections.

It doubles civil penalties for knowing and willful violations, allows disgorgement of funds to the Treasury and community-service remedies, imposes automatic penalties for late reports, and adds expedited pre-election procedures for enforcement complaints.
It bans fundraising solicitations on federal property by any federal official, including the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress, under penalty of fine and imprisonment.
It prohibits officeholders from converting campaign money to personal use such as mortgage payments, clothing, tuition, vacations, or country club dues.
It restricts franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings by Members of Congress during an election year, strengthens the ban on foreign-national contributions, and prohibits contributions by minors.

It requires corporations to obtain separate prior written authorization before using shareholder or employee payments for political activity, gives shareholders an annual objection and pro-rata refund right, and requires unions to get separate, revocable written authorization from members before using dues for politics.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, national and state party committees would lose their unregulated soft money channel, large donors would face the end of unlimited party contributions, corporations and unions would bear new consent, notice, and objection procedures before spending dues or shareholder money on politics, and officeholders would lose election-year franked mass mailings, the ability to raise money on federal property, and the ability to spend campaign funds personally.
analysis.who_pays_short: Party committees, big donors, corporations, unions, incumbents

drawbacks.text: The bill partly pays for its soft money ban by loosening hard money limits: it raises the aggregate individual contribution cap from $25,000 to $30,000 and creates a new $10,000 annual limit for contributions to state party committees, so large donors gain a bigger legal channel even as the unregulated one closes.

The $50,000 personal-funds limit for House candidates is voluntary: a self-funded candidate who simply does not file the declaration faces no cap at all, so the provision does little against the wealthiest candidates.

The new requirement that corporations get separate written consent and that unions get revocable member authorization before using dues for politics would impose significant compliance paperwork, and the shareholder pro-rata objection mechanism requires annual notice-and-response processes for every corporation that spends on politics.

The express-advocacy definition relies on a fixed list of phrases and a 60-day window, so advertising designed to sit just outside that language and timing could still escape contribution limits and coordination rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance this was a well-aimed reform package: the soft money ban, the 24-hour online disclosure rule, the coordination definitions, and the doubled penalties each targeted a loophole that in 1998 let large donors and parties influence elections outside the rules voters could see. The main honest tradeoff is that it partially paid for the soft money ban by raising individual contribution limits, and its voluntary self-funding cap does nothing about the wealthiest candidates who decline it. The prior-authorization and shareholder-objection provisions are real compliance burdens, though they extend to individuals rights over their own money that most would consider basic. The bill's biggest weakness was not its design but its fate: it never got a hearing, so none of these design questions were ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single sponsor, sent to three House committees, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Representative Charles Bass (R-NH) introduced the Campaign Reform Act of 1998 in the House on April 23, 1998 as an amendment to the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971.
No other member signed on; the bill ended with zero cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to the House Oversight Committee and additionally to the Judiciary and Government Reform and Oversight Committees, and on April 29, 1998 the House Oversight Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology received the referral.
No further action of any kind was taken for the remaining eight months of the Congress: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

The bill would have banned soft money for national party committees, required state and local parties to fund federal election activity from regulated money, barred party fundraising for tax-exempt 501(c) organizations, and required 24-hour internet posting of campaign reports.

It would also have doubled penalties for knowing and willful campaign finance violations, banned fundraising on federal property by the President, Vice President, and Members of Congress, barred conversion of campaign funds to personal use, and restricted election-year franked mass mailings.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Political parties keeping their unregulated soft money channels, large donors who preferred contributions outside federal limits, tax-exempt groups that received party money, and incumbents keeping election-year franked mail and access to donors on federal property were all better off because the bill never advanced. Voters lost the 24-hour online disclosure and the stronger penalty regime it would have created.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors and no votes of any kind, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition appears.

industries.note: The bill bans national parties from handling any funds outside federal limits, bars them from raising money for tax-exempt 501(c) groups, and forces state and local parties to pay for federal election activity out of reported, limited hard money. Parties would lose their largest unregulated funding channel.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and soft-money contributors
industries.note: Soft money, their main unregulated channel, would be banned, but the aggregate individual limit would rise from $25,000 to $30,000 and a new $10,000 annual channel to state party committees would open. Wealthy donors would trade a bigger but regulated role for the loss of an unlimited hidden one.

Corporations could no longer use shareholder or employee payments for political activity without separate written consent, and shareholders could annually object and claim their pro-rata share. The corporation's political arm loses a quiet source of funds; shareholders gain control over their own money.

Unions would need separate, revocable written authorization from each member before using dues for politics. Unions have historically opposed such requirements as burdens on member-funded political speech, while the provision's stated aim is individual member control.

Party committees would be barred from soliciting funds for or directing donations to 501(c) organizations, and any person spending over $50,000 on federal election activity would have to file disclosure reports. The bill narrows a route by which party money moved through outside groups without disclosure.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (President, Vice President, Members of Congress)
industries.note: Officeholders could no longer solicit money on federal property, Members could not send taxpayer-funded franked mass mailings during their own election years, and campaign funds could not be spent on personal expenses. Each restriction reduces a perk of holding office.

Advertising would face stronger disclaimer rules: readable boxed print disclosures on the sponsor's identity, a spoken candidate approval statement, and an on-screen sponsor credit for non-candidate ads. No spending limits would be imposed, only identification requirements.
